extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, advocates, stakeholders, and members of the public submitting comments on DHS public charge rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed DHS regulation establishing standards, forms, procedures, fees, and processes for deciding whether an alien is inadmissible as likely to become a public charge, including exemptions, affidavit-of-support rules, Form I-944 data collection, and a public charge bond process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors for public charge determination
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining if an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge, consular and immigration officers must, at a minimum, consider certain factors including the alien’s age, health, and family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills. Additionally, DHS may consider any affidavit of support submitted under section 213A of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the baseline factors the rule relies on; DHS proposes to collect information on these factors via Form I-944 to determine inadmissibility under public charge. (Original wording preserved: "at a minimum, consider certain factors including the alien’s age, health, and family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills." )

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-944 submission requirement for adjustment applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS is proposing a new form—Form I-944—which would collect information based on factors such as age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; education and skills; and any additional financial support through an affidavit of support, so that DHS could determine whether an applicant applying for adjustment of status who is subject to public charge review would be inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the analysis DHS assumes all individuals who apply for adjustment of status using Form I-485 are required to submit Form I-944, unless in a class exempt from review for public charge. The form is intended to operationalize the statutory factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (Form I-864) requirements and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Form I-864 (Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA) is filed to show that applicants have adequate means of financial support; when a sponsor completes and signs Form I-864 the sponsor agrees to use his or her resources, financial or otherwise, to support the intending immigrant named in the affidavit, if it becomes necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affidavit of support creates a legally enforceable obligation between the sponsor and the U.S. Government. DHS may consider any affidavit of support submitted under section 213A when determining whether the applicant may become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-864A and household member contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Form I-864 includes an attachment, Contract Between Sponsor and Household Member (Form I-864A), which may be filed when a sponsor’s income and assets do not meet the income requirements and the qualifying household member chooses to combine his or her resources with the sponsor to meet those requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sponsor must file a separate Form I-864A for each household member whose income/assets are used, and the Form I-864A serves as a contractual agreement that the household member, along with the sponsor, is responsible for providing financial/material support to the sponsored immigrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-864EZ eligibility conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sponsors may file Form I-864EZ, a shorter version of Form I-864, only if: (1) the sponsor is the person who filed or is filing a Petition for Alien Relative (Form I-130) for the relative being sponsored; (2) the relative being sponsored is the only person listed on Form I-130; and (3) the income the sponsor is using for qualification is based entirely on salary or pension and is shown on one or more IRS Form W-2s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form I-864EZ simplifies affidavit-of-support filing but is limited to the specific narrow circumstances above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint sponsor rules for affidavits of support
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual may meet the affidavit-of-support requirement by obtaining a joint sponsor willing to accept joint and several liability with the petitioning sponsor. The joint sponsor must demonstrate income or assets that independently meet the requirements; the joint sponsor’s income/assets may not be combined with those of the petitioning sponsor or the sponsored immigrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both petitioning sponsor and joint sponsor must each complete a Form I-864; joint sponsorship requires showing independent qualifying income/assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from public charge inadmissibility (classes of admission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain classes of applicants for admission, adjustment of status, or registry are exempt from inadmissibility based on public charge grounds. Table 39 lists exemptions including: refugees and asylees at time of admission/grant; Afghan and Iraqi interpreters or nationals employed by or on behalf of the U.S. Government; Cuban Adjustment Act applicants; Haitian HRIFA applicants; Amerasians; Cuban and Haitian entrants under IRCA; Nicaraguans and certain Central Americans under NACARA; Lautenberg parolees; special immigrant juveniles; TPS applicants re-registration; T and U nonimmigrants (per certain statutes); VAWA self-petitioners; qualified aliens under certain PRWORA provisions; nationals adjusting under other named statutory programs; registry applicants; certain parolees (Polish/Hungarian), and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant is in one of these classes, the public charge ground of inadmissibility does not apply. DHS removed these exempt classes when estimating populations subject to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from requirement to submit an affidavit of support
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to exemptions from inadmissibility, certain classes of admission are exempt from the requirement to submit an affidavit of support for applicants for admission, adjustment of status, or registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 41 (referenced) shows populations exempt from the affidavit requirement; when an affidavit is required and submitted it creates a contractual obligation (Form I-864) enforceable by the U.S. Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee waiver eligibility for Form I-485
rubrics_metrics.description: Some applicants seeking adjustment of status may be eligible for a fee waiver for Form I-485 by filing a Request for Fee Waiver (Form I-912). A fee waiver is only available if the applicant is applying for adjustment of status based on certain exempt or specified grounds such as: Special Immigrant Status based on an approved Form I-360 as an Afghan or Iraqi Interpreter or Afghan/Iraqi national employed by or on behalf of the U.S. Government; an adjustment provision exempt from public charge (e.g., Cuban Adjustment Act, HRIFA, NACARA); continuous residence since before Jan. 1, 1972 (Registry); Asylum Status; Special Immigrant Juvenile Status; Lautenberg parolees; and additionally for battered spouses, certain T or U nonimmigrants, or VAWA self–petitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Form I-912 is approved, both the filing fee and biometric services fee are waived; DHS assumes fee waivers are applied in cost analysis where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for nonimmigrant extension/change of status applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Any alien applying for an extension of stay or change of status as a nonimmigrant in the United States would be required to demonstrate that he or she is neither using nor receiving, nor likely to receive, public benefits as defined in this proposed rule unless the applicant is in a class of admission exempt from inadmissibility on public charge grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule extends public charge review to certain nonimmigrant EOS/COS applications, subject to statutory exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond process and related CFR amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to amend 8 CFR 103.6 to set forth the Secretary’s discretion to approve bonds, cancellation, bond schedules, and breach of bond, and to move principles governing public charge bonds to proposed 8 CFR 213.1. DHS would establish a public charge bond process that includes DHS acceptance of a public charge bond posted on an adjustment applicant’s behalf if the applicant was deemed inadmissible based on public charge, the possibility to substitute an existing bond, the requirement to substitute a bond before the bond on file expires, DHS determination of breach of a public charge bond, appeal upon breach determination, cancellation of a public charge bond, and appeal upon denial of cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS currently has authority but no specific process; the proposed rule would create procedures and appeals for bonds, and new forms (Form I-945 public charge bond; Form I-356 request for cancellation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and surety costs associated with public charge bonds and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantified costs include: $0.34 million annually to obligors for submitting Public Charge Bond (Form I-945); $825 to annual filers for submitting Request for Cancellation of Public Charge Bond (Form I-356); fees paid to surety bond companies to secure public charge bond could range from 1–15 percent of the public charge bond amount based on an individual’s credit score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS also reports other cost items (annualized monetized costs at 3% discount: $82,772,721 primary estimate; 7% discount same nominal) and assumes reading the proposed rule takes 8–10 hours per individual for familiarization. These numbers are part of the OMB A-4 accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-4 accounting categories to use for benefits/costs
rubrics_metrics.description: As required by OMB Circular A-4, DHS prepares an accounting statement showing costs associated with the proposed regulation, broken into categories such as monetized benefits, annualized monetized costs (with discount rates), annualized quantified but un-monetized benefits/costs, unquantified benefits and costs, transfers (on-budget/off-budget), and miscellaneous analyses (effects on state/local/tribal governments, small businesses, wages, growth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 37 presents DHS's OMB A-4 Accounting Statement with primary/minimum/maximum estimates and sources; DHS includes both monetized and qualitative (unquantified) effects in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population estimation method for those subject to public charge review
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate populations subject to public charge review, DHS examined the annual total population of individuals who applied for adjustment of status (Form I-485) for fiscal years 2012–2016, removed individuals whose classes of admission are exempt from public charge review (per Table 39), and computed totals and 5-year averages to project annual populations subject to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS used Yearbook of Immigration Statistics data and welcomes public comment on these population estimates and methodology. Example calculation: total 2016 applicants (565,427) minus exempt (182,658) = 382,769 subject to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse qualitative effects to consider in cost analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Other qualitative, unquantified effects of the proposed rule could include potential lost productivity, adverse health effects (including additional medical expenses due to delayed health care treatment), and increased disability insurance claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states it was not able to estimate certain effects quantitatively and notes the lack of academic literature definitively linking immigration to public benefits usage; these qualitative effects are highlighted for comment and consideration.
